title: Cops should reconsider callings suspects, inquest told
article: An inquest jury has recommended York Regional Police and the province take a closer look at whether suspects should be contacted before being arrested.The three-man, two-woman jury made its recommendation after deliberating yesterday in the death of Evan Arnold, 26, of Newmarket, who was shot dead by York police in 2006. The inquest lasted three days at Aurora Town Hall."I'm very happy with the outcome," Mr. Arnold's mother Anne Arnold, an East Gwillimbury resident, told the York Region Media Group."I think it's important that (police) know everything," she said. "So, perhaps they could do it in a better way."On Monday, the inquest heard York police Const. Kelly Morgan contacted Mr. Arnold Sept. 7, 2006, to inform him police planned to arrest him for sexual assault, the inquest heard.Mr. Arnold told the officer he was in Newmarket and walking home, Const. Morgan said, adding Mr. Arnold sounded surprised.He told the officer her call was a "long time coming" and that he was going to "end it all", she said.Const. Morgan didn't know exactly where Mr. Arnold was when they spoke and testified she considered calling for York tactical officers.She had no idea before speaking with Mr. Arnold that afternoon that he was suicidal, she testified.The circumstances surrounding the sexual assault investigation were not discussed during the inquest.Meanwhile, the officer who shot and killed Mr. Arnold had no other choice but to fire, the inquest heard Tuesday.It was 4:16 p.m. Sept. 7, 2006 when York police Const. Jeff Biersteker was called to a break and enter on Southwind Court in Newmarket.What the call developed into was something the officer he never wants to experience again, the inquest heard.Mr. Arnold was inside a home on Southwind, a small residential road southwest of Leslie and Gorham streets.Positioning himself at the left side of a stone porch of the home, Const. Biersteker peered through a sidelight in the front entrance to spot Mr. Arnold in the foyer, the officer testified while under questioning by coroner's counsel Eric Siebenmorgen.Const. Biersteker noticed a large knife in each of his hands, he said.Mr. Arnold was pacing around inside the home and the officer believed the Newmarket man was "talking himself up" or mentally preparing himself.Before the break-in on Southwind, York police had been searching for Mr. Arnold as part of a sexual assault investigation, the inquest heard Monday.As officers, who had surrounded the home, backed off, Mr. Arnold opened the door and stepped out holding the knives, Const. Biersteker said.The officer drew his gun and pointed it at Mr. Arnold's chest as other officers ordered him to drop the knives.Mr. Arnold said he was going to stab police and had tried to harm himself, the officer testified."He also stated he was going to take one of us with him," Const. Biersteker said. "These were not threats I had ever heard before."Brandishing the knives, Mr. Arnold went back into the house and began talking to himself and pacing, the officer testified.Mr. Arnold turned around and walked out the door again, this time across the home's lawn, still holding the knives."He had a purpose," Const. Biersteker said. "He's telling us that he's going to kill us. He turned and locked eyes on me."Mr. Arnold followed Const. Biersteker around a tree and up a slope, the officer testified.As a space behind Mr. Arnold opened, with no fellow officers behind him, Mr. Arnold lunged at Const. Biersteker, the inquest heard."In my estimation, that was him making an attempt to kill me," Const. Biersteker said.He told the inquest he feared for his life and that if he hadn't stopped Mr. Arnold.Const. Biersteker fired twice and struck Mr. Arnold in the chest. Mr. Arnold fell to the ground about eight minutes after Const. Biersteker responded to the call.Mr. Arnold was later pronounced dead at Southlake Regional Health Centre."There is not one single day I haven't thought about it," Const. Biersteker said about shooting Mr. Arnold during cross-examination by police lawyer Joanne Mulcahy. "There was no other option. We're prepared for it, but I hope it never happens again."The shooting was ruled justified by the province's Special Investigations Unit.During a break in testimony, Mr. Arnold's mother Anne Arnold, who has been granted standing at the inquest - meaning she can play an active role in the proceedings and ask questions - approached Const. Biersteker and clasped his hands.She asked the officer not to burden himself with shooting her son."Please, don't carry it around with you," she told him.Const. Biersteker declined comment when the inquest concluded.
